Unfinished Business: Dean Rajan Appointed to Historic Third Term

Madhav Rajan reflects on nine years of leading Chicago Booth and what he wants to accomplish in the years ahead.

  • By Brent White
  • October 05, 2026
  • News
  • Share This Page
Listen to audio version of this article
0:00 / 9:41
Instaread

Two years from now, Madhav Rajan will become the longest-serving dean of Chicago Booth since 1945.

That milestone is not lost on Rajan, the Steven S. Wymer Dean and Distinguished Service Professor of Accounting, who came to Booth from Stanford in 2017 and has led the school through a period of record fundraising, significant endowment growth, and major increases in scholarship funding. He also spearheaded the school’s first new degree programs in nearly 90 years—the Master in Management and the Asness and Liew Master in Finance—all while, for the past year, taking on an additional role as UChicago’s chief global strategist.

Dean Rajan is quick to give the faculty credit for his decision to stay on: Last year, Booth’s tenured faculty unanimously petitioned him to serve a third term—a level of consensus that took him by surprise. “Getting the faculty to agree unanimously on anything is probably my biggest achievement in life,” he jokes. “That to me was the real reason I agreed to a third term. I’m doing it because the faculty wanted it to happen.”

In this Q&A marking his historic reappointment, Dean Rajan reflects on his past accomplishments, plans for his third term, why he thinks an MBA is still a worthwhile investment, and the parallels he sees between a good puzzle and running a complex organization like Booth.

You have a passion for trivia and enjoy a good crossword puzzle. When did these interests begin, and what role have they played in your life?

I started doing trivia seriously in college in India. In my third year, I won every event I entered. Then I moved to the US for my masters and completely gave it up because I didn’t know anything about American pop culture.

I picked it back up years later at Stanford, when someone coaching my teaching told me, “There isn’t anything in your teaching that’s you; pick something you’re passionate about.” So I started incorporating a trivia question into every class. The students loved it so much that on the last day, I did 45 minutes of trivia. I stopped again when I moved to Chicago as dean, until I was asked last year to host trivia for a deans and officers meeting here at UChicago.

I used to do crosswords with my uncle and my mother years ago. That interest really picked up again once I started traveling for this job. I once had a 1,492-day streak of completing The New York Times crossword puzzle. It ended when I was traveling and lost internet access in Egypt. I don’t think I’ll ever replicate that.

What sort of parallels do you see between running a large and complex organization like Booth, and trying to solve a complex crossword puzzle?

This is a complicated organization. Unlike running a company, the objective functions aren’t clear, and the various constituents—students, staff, faculty, alumni, the university—each want something completely different.

Bringing it all to bear in a place where the result is so ambiguous, it really helps to have the patience to go through very complicated things. You have to get used to failing and having the path and process be difficult to get to where you need to go.

Last fall, you spearheaded a partnership with MasterClass for Booth. One year later, 705 people from 55 countries are part of the first cohort of MasterClass Executive. Why is it important to you that Booth develops partnerships like this?

I view MasterClass Executive as a way for us to get further into the nondegree space and in the use of AI for instruction. David Rogier, the CEO of MasterClass, was a student in my accounting class at Stanford. When he reached out, this partnership seemed like an intriguing way to put Booth at the leading edge of the curve. We spoke last September and we now have a program that’s finishing its first cohort. Academic institutions tend to move slowly, but we were both able to move things along because of the trust David and I already had.

For Booth, it’s been great marketing the school to a distinct audience. It’s given our name a completely different luster. Was it risky? Of course. People were worried about brand dilution, but not anymore. And literally every faculty member I spoke to agreed to do it.

Booth has been amazing as a place to try really big ideas and see many of them succeed.

“To me, risk-taking is about having a clear strategic vision of what you’re trying to achieve. It’s about trying to figure out a way around the problems that you’re facing in an innovative way.”

— Dean Rajan

In the university’s announcement about your third term, the provost cited your leadership in taking “smart risks on new ideas.” What’s your personal philosophy on risk-taking? How do you determine which risks are worth taking?

I feel we’ve been more open to risk-taking than our peer institutions, and it’s worked because we’ve been open to shutting things down if they’re not working.

Starting to teach undergrads was a huge risk—our original idea for a business major completely failed, so we took a side turn and created a track in the econ major, which allows undergrads to take electives at Booth. Eight years on, the Business Economics Specialization is the most popular major in the College.

To me, risk-taking is about having a clear strategic vision of what you’re trying to achieve. It’s about trying to figure out a way around the problems that you’re facing in an innovative way. It’s not about copying other people. In addition to those things, we have to have faculty backing and support to move ahead with any new initiative or program. If we don’t have that, it’s doomed to fail.

When you began your first term, you said, “I wanted to be dean at a school where I would be proud to be a faculty member.” What have you learned about the faculty since then?

That statement is still true. The caliber of our faculty, and the level at which they operate, is a completely different level than any of our peer schools. I believe that is the core distinguishing feature of Chicago Booth—the quality of faculty we are able to attract, support, and retain.

We have the best faculty in the world in most of our disciplines, which is amazing for one institution to say. At the margin, all of our resources have gone into preserving that.

In my first faculty meeting here, I told the faculty I was never going to interfere in the way they govern themselves, because I trusted them to have the judgment to do it. And I told them I wanted some big things changed in the school and I wanted their support to do it. I’ve gotten that over the last nine years.

Why do you think an MBA will remain a worthwhile investment, and why do you believe Booth is the best place for future MBA students, given the changes AI is bringing to the labor market?

The great thing about the MBA is that it’s eternally morphable into whatever you need it to be. Our MBA Programs have evolved significantly over the last 10 or 20 years. That’s what makes it the perfect degree, as long as you’re willing to adapt it to the times.

One big advantage we have in AI: Our faculty are leaders at empirical research—that’s what Chicago has always been known for. We’re the best school at working with data in all forms—experimental data, empirical data—taking it, making decisions, and using it to change organizations and society.

In the last two years, the big investments we’ve made have been in computing power, which I would never have guessed. We spend a lot on research professionals who help faculty. As long as we have faculty at the leading edge of research, they’ll bring that into the classroom. You can take a base-level accounting class like people did 20 years ago, or Bradford Levy’s AI and Financial Information class.

We’ll keep adapting our MBA Programs to whatever is needed to best support the students going through them at that time.

As you head toward becoming the longest-serving dean of Booth in more than 80 years, what are the two biggest things you want to get done in the years ahead?

First, I want to find a way to maintain and sustain our part-time programs—the Sokolov Executive MBA Program and the Evening and Weekend MBA Programs. Making structural changes to the way we operate in the US and global markets to ensure success in these programs is, in my view, the single biggest challenge the school faces.

We have great assets—the faculty, the brand, alumni engagement—and leveraging them to get these programs in front of the people who will benefit most is a big goal of mine over the next few years.

Second, we have been the fortunate recipients of significant philanthropic investments by our alumni. I want to continue that momentum through the completion of our capital campaign.  Finding additional sources of funding for faculty research support and student scholarships is critical. My ultimate goal is simple—I want to ensure that the school is financially sustainable for the foreseeable future.
